title: A trial aiming to determine whether giving thiamine (a vitamin) can help prevent or treat delirium in patients who are admitted to intensive care
official: A double-blind randomised clinical trial of supplementary intravenous thiamine versus placebo in the treatment and prevention of delirium in the intensive care unit
summary:
Background and study aims 
Over 50% of patients who are admitted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) will suffer from a condition called delirium (a sudden state of confusion and altered awareness) during their stay. This causes problems with attention, thinking, and memory, and can include frightening hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that only exist in the mind) or delusions.  Delirium is associated with negative outcomes that are important to patients, including longer time spent in the ICU/hospital, increased chance of dying, loss of independent function, and long-term emotional distress.
Researchers believe delirium is caused by brain cells not being able to produce energy properly. Vitamin B1, known as thiamine, is a very safe and cheap medication. We believe giving thiamine to ICU patients could reduce delirium by helping brain cells produce energy, but there is little clinical evidence to support this. The study aims to determine whether thiamine can reduce delirium in ICU patients and improve their recovery. 

Who can participate? 
Patients aged 18 years and over receiving either invasive mechanical ventilation or two or more organ support (defined as respiratory [non-invasive ventilation or high flow nasal oxygen], cardiovascular [new requirement for vasopressor treatment] or renal support [new acute renal replacement therapy]) within 48 hours of ICU admission

What does the study involve? 
This study will compare intravenous thiamine with a placebo (a treatment with no active ingredient). Participants will be randomly allocated to receive either thiamine or placebo, and neither the participants nor the healthcare professionals caring for them will know which treatment has been given. This approach helps ensure that the results are reliable and unbiased. Researchers will assess a range of important health outcomes, including recovery from critical illness, length of stay in hospital, quality of life after discharge, and the safety of the treatment. In addition, blood and urine samples will be analysed to help understand how thiamine may affect the body and brain during critical illness. 

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating? 
The findings from DELTA-ICU may help improve the care of future ICU patients.
Potential risks and benefits of taking part in the trial will be fully detailed in the Patient and Legal Representative Information Sheets.
Thiamine (vitamin B1) is a safe drug, with minimal side effects. Patients in both groups will be closely monitored for serious adverse events that may be related to the trial treatments. Data on serious adverse events will be collected on all study participants. Safety will be monitored by the independent Data Monitoring and Ethics Committee (at a schedule deemed appropriate by the Committee) who will recommend the continuation (or not) of the trial to the majority-independent Trial Steering Committee.
The trial involves biological samples being obtained from all participants. A blood and urine sample will be obtained at baseline, during the intervention and at Day 14 (or discharge from the intensive care unit, whichever is sooner). Most participants due to the critical nature of their illness will have an arterial or central line inserted for their care and a urine drain. Therefore, blood samples will be obtained from inserted lines causing no additional burden to the participant and where possible these will be obtained alongside clinical bloods by trained members of staff.  Urine samples will be obtained from the urine drain, or if no urine drain is in place and the participant is able, they will provide their own sample in a urine pot.
As the trial will use identifiable and health data, there is a small risk that data could be lost or breached. Robust measures will be in place to prevent this from occurring – e.g. through the implementation of regular data backup arrangements and data disaster recovery procedures. All trial data will be entered onto a database (Open Clinica) by the recruiting NHS hospital. Open Clinica is secure and validated for use in clinical trials. Access will be closely controlled by ICNARC Clinical Trials Unit. Identifiable data will only be collected where essential. Participants will be allocated a unique Trial Number to minimise processing of identifiable data. We will use data linkage for routinely collected patient data and additional in-hospital data collection into a case report form. 
One potential perceived burden to patients taking part in the trial could be the completion of follow-up questionnaires at 90 days. The questionnaires will be conducted over the phone and should take no longer than 15 minutes to complete. All information on the follow up questionnaires will be provided on the Patient / Legal Representative Information Sheet participants will be presented with this as an option to consent (or not) for this on the consent form. Our previous studies have achieved response rates ranging 75-80% of critical care survivors.

Where is the study run from? 
Intensive Care National Audit & Research Centre (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
September 2026 to January 2029

Who is funding the study? 
Efficacy and Mechanism Evaluation Programme (UK)

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Adult (aged ≥18 years)
2. Receiving either:
2.1. Invasive mechanical ventilation
2.2. Two or more organ support (defined as respiratory [non-invasive ventilation or high flow nasal oxygen], cardiovascular [new requirement for vasopressor treatment] or renal support [new acute renal replacement therapy])
3. Within 48 hours of ICU admission
Exclusion criteria:
1. Taking prescribed thiamine at the time of ICU admission, by any route, or a clinical indication for supplementary intravenous thiamine, for example: 
1.1. Documented or suspected alcohol dependence - with high risk of Wernicke’s-Korsakoff Syndrome or alcohol withdrawal syndrome on ICU admission
1.2.  Severe or moderate malnutrition on ICU admission with high risk of refeeding syndrome 
2. Known allergy to thiamine
3. Expected to be discharged from ICU within 48 hours
4. Death perceived as imminent or for end of life care only 
5. Neurological injury that prevents assessment of delirium, e.g., traumatic brain injury, intracranial haemorrhage or ischaemic brain injury from stroke or hypoperfusion
6. Pre-existing neurocognitive disorders that prevent the assessment of delirium, e.g., severe dementia, severe learning difficulties
7. Confirmed pregnancy or breastfeeding
